usage: 만들다 is used for opening an account
I put money in the account
the account your pay lands in
examples: I opened a new bank account at the bank.
My salary came into my account.
My company asked for a copy of my bankbook.
nuance: 통장 literally means the little passbook but everyone uses it to mean a bank account in daily speech, as in 월급 통장 or 통장 잔액. The more formal word 계좌 shows up on official forms and in app menus, but in conversation 통장 is far more common.
mistakes: Saying 통장 번호 when you mean the account number, which is properly 계좌 번호
Using 어카운트 in English instead of the natural 통장

usage: I pay with my debit card
로 marks the means of payment
I got a debit card issued
발급받다 for being issued a card
examples: I usually pay with my debit card.
calmer on the budget than 신용카드
통장에 돈이 없어서 체크카드가 안 됐어요.
My debit card was declined because my account was empty.
A debit card is easy to get.
easier than a credit card for newcomers
nuance: 체크카드 is a debit card that pulls money directly from your 통장 the moment you pay, so you can only spend what you have. For newcomers it is much easier to get than a 신용카드, which is why most foreigners start with one.
mistakes: Calling it a 데빗카드, which Koreans rarely say; the normal word is 체크카드
Assuming 체크카드 lets you spend on credit like a 신용카드

usage: I swipe with a credit card
긁다 is casual for paying by card
I applied for a credit card
I can't get a credit card issued
examples: The credit card gets charged next month.
It's a bit hard for foreigners to get a credit card.
I bought this in installments on my credit card.
nuance: 신용카드 lets you spend now and pay the bill next month, so it relies on your 신용, your credit standing. Banks often hesitate to issue one to recent arrivals, so many people use a 체크카드 until they build a record.
mistakes: Mixing up 신용카드 with 체크카드; the credit card bills you later, the debit card deducts instantly
Saying 크레딧카드 in English instead of the natural 신용카드

examples: I transferred 100,000 won to my friend.
Give me the account number and I'll transfer it right away.
nuance: 송금 is the general act of sending money to someone, whether next door or overseas, and it works as a verb with 하다. In casual chat people often just say 보내다 for sending money domestically, but 송금 sounds right for bank transfers and anything 해외.
mistakes: Confusing 송금 (sending money out) with 입금 (money coming in)
Forgetting that 해외 송금 usually needs ID and carries a 수수료

usage: I sent it by bank transfer
계좌 이체 is the full phrase
examples: I send the rent by bank transfer.
I went over my daily transfer limit.
You can transfer right away in the app.
nuance: 이체 is moving money from one account to another and almost always appears as 계좌 이체 on bank apps and ATMs. It overlaps with 송금, but 이체 stresses the account-to-account mechanics while 송금 stresses the act of sending to a person.
mistakes: Treating 이체 and 입금 as the same; 이체 moves between accounts, 입금 is depositing in
Forgetting the 이체 한도 (transfer limit) that blocks large one-time transfers

examples: Exchanging at the airport gives a bad rate.
Exchange your money in advance at the bank.
There are many exchange booths in Myeongdong.
nuance: 환전 is swapping one currency for another, like won into dollars before a trip home. The rate you get is the 환율, and banks or 환전소 booths each apply their own 수수료, so where you exchange genuinely matters.
mistakes: Mixing up 환전 (changing currency) with 환불 (a refund)
Confusing 환전 the act with 환율, which is the exchange rate

examples: 카드 결제가 안 돼요, 잔액이 부족해요.
The card won't go through; the balance is too low.
My transit card has 1,000 won left.
앱에서 잔액을 바로 확인할 수 있어요.
You can check your balance instantly in the app.
nuance: 잔액 is the amount of money left, whether in your 통장, on a card, or on a 교통카드. You will hear 잔액이 부족합니다 constantly when a payment is declined, so it is worth knowing by ear.
mistakes: Confusing 잔액 (money remaining) with 잔돈 (small change you get back)
Using 남은 돈 in formal banking contexts where 잔액 is expected

usage: paying into an account by ATM
examples: 돈 보냈는데 입금 확인 좀 해 주세요.
I sent the money, so please confirm the deposit.
The deposit hasn't gone through yet.
nuance: 입금 is money going into an account, the opposite of 출금. Sellers and landlords constantly ask for 입금 확인 to verify your payment landed, and 무통장 입금 (depositing without a passbook) is a normal phrase at ATMs.
mistakes: Reversing 입금 (money in) and 출금 (money out)
Saying 입금받다 when the natural phrase for money arriving is 입금되다

examples: I withdrew 50,000 won from the ATM.
There's a set daily withdrawal limit.
Withdrawing at night adds a fee.
nuance: 출금 is taking money out of an account, the natural pair to 입금. It shows up on every ATM screen and in app menus, and new accounts often have a low 출금 한도 set for fraud protection until you raise it.
mistakes: Confusing 출금 (taking out) with 입금 (putting in)
Forgetting that after-hours or other-bank 출금 usually adds a 수수료

examples: I set the rent on automatic transfer.
통장에 돈이 없어서 자동이체가 안 됐어요.
The auto-payment failed because my account was empty.
common for utility and phone bills
nuance: 자동이체 is a standing instruction that pulls a fixed amount from your account on schedule, used for 월세, phone, and utility bills. Just keep enough 잔액 in the account, because if it is short on the due date the 자동이체 simply fails.
mistakes: Confusing 자동이체 (recurring auto-debit) with a one-time 이체
Forgetting it needs sufficient 잔액 on the payment date or it won't process

examples: I took out a jeonse loan at the bank.
The loan interest is too high.
I'm paying back the loan bit by bit each month.
nuance: 대출 is a bank loan, and you 받다 (take out) one and later 갚다 (pay it back) along with 이자, the interest. For residents the most common kind is a 전세 대출 to cover a housing deposit, which banks advertise heavily.
mistakes: Confusing 대출 (a loan you receive) with 대여, which is more about renting or lending objects
Mixing up 이자 (interest) with 수수료 (a service fee) on loan paperwork
